Sermon I: *monopeda* is a rare, obscure word and the edition has a footnote mark on it; 'one-footed carriage' is a guess from the sense. *Argutatum* ('cunningly contrived') is doubtful. The words 'nisi mavis agitatum, aut quidlibet aliud' ('unless you prefer agitatum, or anything else'), printed in the opening of Sermon II, appear to be the editor's footnote on this word, displaced into the text; they are left out of the translation. 'Sequi navigio' could also mean 'follow by boat', which suits the context less well. The first word of 'Then the Lord of powers' is illegible (it ends in -e), and 'Then' is supplied from the sense. In 'et in navicula et super unda', the phrase may instead go with 'I presumed to come to you'. Sermon III: 'e s(??)nelo Evangelio' is taken as 'e sancto Evangelio'. 'Chanan' is rendered Cana. The edition marks gaps in the text, shown here as [...]; the sentences 'invitato Jesu [...] dum vino luxuriæ defecerunt' and 'quæ [...] Christo' are incomplete, and their sense is uncertain. *Instrumento* ('furnishing'), which also carries a footnote mark, is doubtful. The syntax of 'adulterum demutata maritum' is compressed; '[her husband]' is supplied.

Text is lacunose throughout III.3-4 (dots in the edition); III.4 'An oblitus es matrem ... praestigium' is too broken for connected sense, and only the legible words are given. III.3: 'elavus' read as 'clavus' (nail). 'Equidem non potest nisi germen germini obviare' is obscure and possibly corrupt; the parenthesis is the edition's. 'ut constiterit de botruo pendente' is uncertain; the sense may instead be that she will stand by the hanging cluster. III.4: 'merificat' is a rare verb, apparently from 'merum' (unmixed wine). 'Jesu' is taken as nominative. III.5: 'vitavit' may be corrupt for 'invitavit' (he who invited) or 'vitiavit' (he who corrupted, i.e. the devil); it is translated as printed. 'fecunda' (fertile) makes a weak contrast with 'formosa', and 'foeda' (foul) may be meant. III.6: the damaged word before 'acceperunt' is taken as 'illa' (those). IV.2: 'incommodum' is marked by the editor and its sense here is doubtful; 'sensus mei dicentis' and 'detinebantur in corde plantaria' are awkward and may be corrupt. 'diustius suppurgatum' is read as 'diutius suppuratum' (festered longer); this is conjectural.

5.3: 'Pro eo quod domus sua deserta sit' loosely recalls Haggai 1:9-11; 'in matutinis' is taken as the morning office (Matins). 5.4: the text is broken at 'terra dar.... dicere', so the words about the land and what follows cannot be recovered with confidence; 'humo' is read as 'homo', and 'ut plus si' as 'ut plus sit'. The sentence as transmitted says the Jew is more sacrilegious than the Christian is devout, which is an awkward comparison and may be corrupt; the sense wanted seems to be that the Jew in his sacrilegious observance is more zealous than the Christian in his religion. 5.5: 'manicare' is taken as late Latin 'to rise early, come early'; 'Jabo' is read as 'dabo'.

nodes.text: FIRST SERMON.
On the Gospel passage where blessed Peter endured a storm at sea in the boat. Matthew 14:22 ff.

When a swallow prepares her fledged chicks for the art of flying, she lets them go a little way into the air, yet stays close to them herself, lest they should perhaps fall in their fright, being still weak at flying. So too our Saviour Jesus Christ sent out his disciples, like tender chicks, from the little nests of rest, to be tested by the waves of the sea. But when the sea squall began to throw the wings of their devotion into confusion, and the windy storm to scatter them, he who commands the wind has the power to follow the boat. He made for himself a most mighty *monopeda* [a one-footed carriage], a unique four-horse chariot, laying out with his footprints a wondrous street, not adorned with marble but painted with waves, [paved] not with stones but with the soles of his feet. He who mercifully sent them ahead does not withdraw far. They went on alone and not alone, to be tempted, to be proved, to be visited. Like a cunning thief and housebreaker, the one who stirs up the storm, who does not love calm, found his opportunity; and, as though the Master were absent, he tempts the disciples, blows up the winds, rouses the sea, and does not see the helmsman following. With their lord absent, a shipwreck is cunningly contrived against the servants without cause, but the vessel is held fast by mercy. Meanwhile they stretch out their hands, pour out tears, lower the sails; the ropes and cables shriek, that Peter may be set loose and the devil bound. Where, they cry out, it says, Lord, are you, our Saviour? You sent us ahead, and you have abandoned us. Here is the wrecker: where are you, most mighty helmsman? Here is the storm: where are you, mercy? Here the sea is barking: where are you, Lamb of God, who took away the sins of the world?

At once the Lord arrives, smiling with mercy at the tender chicks. When the troubling winds have been scattered, he comes with power, addresses them with gentleness, and with wisdom restores his own as well. They see and are troubled, who were troubled by not seeing. O things beyond telling, my brothers! Fear everywhere, either from danger or from miracle. But he who calmed the storm took away their fear. Do not be afraid, he says; it is I. Great comfort comes to them from the Lord's making known who he is. Lord, they cry: we are safe, if it is you; we are not afraid, if it is you. And Peter says: I can do what you are doing, if it is you; but prove to me truly if it is you, and command me to come over the waters, if it is you. Lord, I have spoken to you: without you I have not presumed; I said, if you command; but [I shall do] what I said only if you help. If you do not help, do not command; but if you help, deign to command, and command me to come to you over the waters. And the Lord in reply: Come to me, if you presume on me. The Lord was glad, and with a joyful face showed his favour, waiting for his fisherman, his confessor, his bold presumer, his leader, his great companion, and his first carbuncle, his precious stone; waiting not far off but near, because of his mercy.

So the sea slips from under Peter as he trembles. The sea sensed faith failing in Peter, and began to bark with a greater tongue of waves. What had been made firm is loosened, because the firm foundation of faith was loosened. Like wax melted by the hot sun, so the softened wave began to give way. Peter felt the rock of the deep totter, now weak and turning to liquid; and with his footsteps sinking and his limbs quivering, with his palms stretched out, he cries out and says: Help me, Lord, and have mercy on me. I always have fear without you, both in the boat and on the wave; I presumed to come to you. Why should I be taken away from you? Help me, call me back to the ship, climb aboard with me, let me come with you. [Then] the Lord of powers, who is with us, our upholder, the God of Jacob, lifted Peter up, steadied him, made him walk unafraid, restored the trembling disciples, quelled the squall, steered the little boat. May he calm the Church herself, his bride and our mother; and amid this storm may we always have as helmsman the one whom Peter had as defender! Amen.
SERMON II.
How much fasting avails.

Moses fasted for forty days and forty nights in the wilderness, that he might be worthy to receive the law of the Lord. Fasts obtained what a full belly despaired of. See then, dearest brothers, what difference there is between fasting and fullness, between an empty belly and lungs seething with feasts. Moses, because he fasted, saw the Lord; and the people, because they ate and drank, made idols. Why do I speak of Moses and of the multitude of Israel? Adam himself, the first of our race, was in paradise as long as he did not eat; as soon as he ate, he was cast out of paradise. He who had been a virgin in the paradise of God, once cast out of paradise knew his wife; for wantonness is always joined to fullness: the parts of the body for gorging and for lust are neighbours to each other; the order of the vices follows the order of the body's parts.

Holy Elijah, whom the elements served, who had shut up the sky for three years and six months, at whose voice fire came down from above, when Jezebel wanted to kill him and he lay exhausted under a shady tree in the wilderness, an angel is sent to him, and he commanded him to take a little bread and water; for he was to set out through the desert to Mount Sinai on a fast of forty days. Could not the almighty Lord, who had made heaven and earth, to whom all creation belongs, have sent by the angel honeyed wine or wines, or seasoned foods, or delicacies of the sea, or the dainties of birds? But he knew that his prophet could not overcome the temptations of the devil unless he were schooled by fasts.

Food, dearest brothers, cast us out of paradise; let hunger lead us back. That Daniel who knew things to come, the clearest herald both of the Lord's coming and of the overthrow of Jerusalem, was called a man of desires for this reason: that he did not eat the bread of desire and did not drink the drink of lust; for he desired Christ more than feasts. John, the forerunner of the Lord, was fed on locusts in the wilderness, not on the flesh of animals and the dainties of birds. He could certainly have provided himself with delicacies of fish beside the streams of the Jordan; but since he was to preach repentance, he had to teach the doctrine of austerity and fasting by his own example more than by his voice. When in the Gospel a certain man full of a demon had been brought to the Lord, whom the apostles could not cleanse, they ask and hear: This kind is not cast out except by prayers and fasts.

See, brothers, how great is the power of fasts, that fasts can do what the apostles could not. Let the old examples be set aside; let each one consider himself and weigh how great is the difference in praying between an empty belly and a fed one, between a flushed face and a pale mouth, between virgin saliva and lips slack from drinking bouts, between a mind weighed down with feasts and one kept alert by the leanness of going without food. I do not speak of double and multiplied fasts, I do not speak of weeks, but let us at least pass single days without luxury of food. Let baths, wines and delicacies cease; not that we judge God's creation to be condemned, but that we who have lived for ourselves the whole year may be able to live for God at least for a few days, with the help of him who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit for ever and ever. Amen.
SERMON III.
On the Gospel passage where the Lord made wine from water. John, chapter 2.

A wedding, at which Christ reclined as both giver and guest: giver, that is, at the origin, and made a guest in [our] kind, so that he who at the beginning of the new union had granted that man be born of man might himself also deign to be born of a virgin [...] Our ears, struck, have now resounded from the holy Gospel: On the third day, it says, a wedding took place in Cana of Galilee, and the mother of Jesus was there; and Jesus was invited with his disciples to the wedding. If the lurking foulness of the Manichaeans' voluptuous depravity is questioned about marriage, God, it says, did not make it. If, then, God did not make marriage, how did Christ recline at it, invited with his disciples? But now let us fan away the cloud of this dark mystery. On the third day, it says, a wedding took place in Cana of Galilee. So when the day of the Trinity was shining over the world, darkened by obscuring sins, Christ came to the wedding. At that time the soul, which had already been chafed by partnership with the clay and through the fornication of the delightful fruit had exchanged [her husband] for an adulterous husband, was celebrating the wedding of a polluted union. Hear Paul dreading the bonds of this evil marriage once more: I fear, he says, that as the serpent deceived Eve by his cunning, so your minds may be corrupted from the simplicity and chastity which is in Christ Jesus our Lord. So while the devil and the soul, tossed on the furnishing of a single couch, were wanton, Jesus being invited [...] when they ran short of the wine of lust. But that mother of Christ, who shrank in horror from the pact of a criminal union, who remained a virgin not only in body but also in mind, was present as a guest, by the condition of [her] kind, not by sharing in the crime, by the universal lot of being born, not by fellowship in sinning, she who [...] to Christ, not one who would consent to the pleasant world.

So this mother of Christ, pitying the long toil of the world, who knew that from the vine-shoot of faith she had drawn a great [...] cluster, began to ask wine of her own offspring. Now when she believed the angel, then she made her plea for the world: then she began to plead the cause of the age, when she did not tremble at the message. For behold the handmaid of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word. Soon, propagated from the seed of the Holy Spirit in the virginal woodland, the first vine blossomed, which, shaded by heavenly bowers, put out leaves beneath [...] and brought forth a hidden cluster. Salvation hung on the tip of faith, and the cluster swelled [...]. See, afterwards from the womb of the mother the bunch of divine offspring, given life [...], was born. Christ, the true cluster, indeed held within himself the wine of life [...] the press of the cross had come near. His mother says: They have no wine. O most wise virgin! Only now have you been found worthy to bring forth the offspring that has sprouted, and already you want to press out the cluster [...]? Indeed a shoot can only oppose a shoot and resist (its own vine-branch). But he who plucked punishment from a tree must await the remedy on a tree; and he who reaped forbidden fruit on a tree must wait at the cross, so that where [...] he had drunk in dryness, there he may receive the drink of salvation. They have no wine, she says. Wait a little, virgin: let the Jew prepare the wood, let the nail go down into the cluster, and [...] the wine will be able [...]. Why do you run to the vat before the time, when Judas has not yet pressed his insolent heel upon the grape? For this is that Judas, destroyer of the sacred vintage, who, having bargained for thirty pieces of silver, sold the cluster of divine offspring to the [...] impious Jews. Of him it had already been sung in the psalms: For even the man of my peace, in whom I hoped, who ate my bread, has enlarged his heel against me. The appointed day will come, virgin, when your fruit is pressed and a sword passes through your own soul, so that it may be made plain concerning the hanging cluster which you had poured forth from the root.

They have no wine, she says. And Jesus [says]: What is there between me and you, woman? My hour has not yet come [...]. Surely the hour not of fate but of vow, not of necessity imposed but of will freely spent [...] not one at which he would be forced to die, but one at which he would deign to die for the world. What is there between me and you, woman? Or have you forgotten your mother? [...] Or do you set your power apart? [...] Have you nothing in common with your mother? Or [...] your eyes [...] majesty? Do you designate yourself Creator? Or [...] now [...] to drive away [...] impulse [...] most wicked [...] perished [...] work while with [...] trick. Here Christ raised his divinity above his mother. He did not deny his mother, nor did he deny that he was born of flesh, but he subjected his mother to his majesty. And therefore he says: What is there between me and you, woman? My hour has not yet come. For in the miracle the deity is proclaimed higher than the mother; but in the hour, the sharing of death is made known. Meanwhile Christ turns tasteless draughts into pure wine: insipid water was poured into the jars, and intoxicating streams were drawn out. What is this so sudden conversion? Wine is born in water, flavour rises secretly in the liquid: sweetness sprouts in wines, and nowhere does a vine bear fruit; no grape is pressed, and wines ferment without a vine-shoot.

O the beauty of a great miracle! The powers of the divine command are grafted in, and fruit is born in water. Christ did in the water what he does at a fixed season in the vine. For who else weds the root to the rain? Who else, through the hidden fibres of its veins, entwines the star-shaped vine-shoots? Who fattens the swelling clusters, budded as if into tips, except him who calls forth and multiplies all things? so that what is bound up in the seed spreads out in the shoot, and what lies hidden in the grain runs wild in leaf. Meanwhile the Church, who at the table of the age reclined polluted with another's husband, is rewarded by Christ with sudden draughts. The wedding passes to Christ. For he who shunned [it] himself gave the dowry. Christ seized the banquet, and the Church changed bridegroom. Christ gave food, and the enemy was shut out. He mixed the drink of his own blood, and took a wife. I have fitted you, says the apostle, to one husband, to present a chaste virgin to Christ. See, she who was once fertile is now beautiful, formerly an adulteress, now a matron; she stands at the right hand of God in gilded clothing, wrapped about with many colours, cleansed through water, dyed purple through blood, made white through the resurrection of the Lord, adorned in many colours with the precious gems of grace: and as Scripture has said, her eyes are tawny from wine, and her teeth are whiter than milk. So let us too drink her wine with her milk, if we wish both to grow beautiful in faith, and to grow white in virtue, and to shine in the adornment of the holy Church.

Receive another great mystery from a small one. Once Judaea too had no wine at her banquet, because she did not receive the gift of the consecrated blood; and while she was marrying the Law, she found nothing at all to drink. Christ came, he changed law into grace, the former a puffer-up, the latter a helper. He poured into the Law the cup of blood, and by dying he made a banquet. The steward of the feast, that is, the Lord of the world, tasted the water made wine and says: Every man sets out the good wine first, and when men have become drunk, that which is worse; but you have kept the good wine until now. For the Law too is holy, as the commandment is holy and just and good; but the Law and the prophets prophesied until John; and so at the coming of the Lord the Mosaic wines failed, and the wines of blood flowed forth. Those [...] received their end, these took their beginning. In short, this is the beginning of the signs which Jesus did, when, slain, he fed the nations, and, wounded, made a banquet from the wine of his blood.

This cluster, sprung up in the land of promise or in the turf of virginity, the Jew once fixed on a carrying-pole, as if in a foreshadowing of the cross to come, to be bent beneath it, not to be refreshed by it. For already the psalm had spoken of them beforehand: Let their eyes be darkened so that they do not see, and bend their back always. So two men carried the cluster, one in front and the other behind; in the middle hung the offspring of the vine-shoot's growth. The first indicated the people of the Jews, the second represented the people of the Gentiles. The Jew indeed went ahead, but he set his back against the cluster. The Gentile walked behind, but he attended to the cluster with the eyes of faith, because he believed in the one hanging. They have turned, says the Lord concerning the Jews, their backs to me and not their faces. The first turned away, the second was fed; the one panted under the burden of sin, the other drank from heaven. So for the Jew the cluster was behind, for the Gentile in front; for them at the end, for us at the beginning; them it pursued to punishment, us it invited to food. And so they were dried up and withered, but we have eaten and drunk and been refreshed, through the same Jesus Christ who lives with the Father and with the Holy Spirit for ever and ever. Amen.
SERMON IV.
On the daily Mass.

The gathering of your blessedness, dearest brothers, makes us filled with exceeding joy. But because my breast, bound by the chains of the body, is afraid, I cannot say how much the splendour of your mind delights to hear. Yet I make the attempt, since, with the pledge given by God growing brighter and the token of most splendid light shining back, the mind of me, the speaker, quivers. I ask that you implant in your ears, my brothers, the duties of a priest, by which through the bowels of mercy he will not cease to labour in birth at what is troublesome, as the apostle Paul says: My little children, with whom I am in labour again, until Christ is formed in you. But the apostle says this to those who, as first-fruits of a new faith and a still raw belief, were kept as seedlings in the heart. But, God being gracious, because among you the privilege of faith so grows old that it is also new, it therefore keeps its newness in order to be old: for thus it is written: Good wine grows old, and will be drunk with sweetness. Yet I could not conceal what has festered even longer. I did not want to see what I should mourn, I did not want to see what I should grieve over. I cry out because I am a shepherd, not a hireling, who at the sight of the wolf flees and abandons the sheep to perish. I cry out because I fear, I cry out because I grieve: for by crying out I both excuse myself and do not lose you. For if I keep silent, I both do not excuse myself and lose you. For God says through the prophet Isaiah: Cry out, he says, in your strength, and do not spare: raise your voice like a trumpet, announce to my people their sins, and to the house of Jacob their crimes. For your devotion has so grown cold, my brothers, that I both perceive and fear this: what the Lord says, because crime abounds the charity of many grows cold, I think is being fulfilled in your devotion. For while you make it your practice to sit in your houses, you make the house of God deserted.

And hear how, through the prophet, divine indignation of this kind rebukes the minds of all. Hear, Christian, what you should fear; hear, God-fearing one, what you should beware of: Because his house is deserted, therefore the sky will withhold its rains, and the earth will not give its fruit, and I will bring the sword upon the works of men's hands, because God is not heard in the churches. Who, my brothers, attending to this, would not tremble in his innermost parts? Who, struck by such great threats, would not wither, when he hears the Lord thus indignant because you make his house deserted, and the house of prayer is empty of the religious assembly? The street is full of people, and the church is silent. Surely, prudent man, you are not told to gather at the house of God at every hour. If at Matins there is scarcely one hour, if on feast days there are scarcely two hours, see, it is little that your maker demands of you. And do you not want to be blessed? You want the sky and the earth, the sea and all the elements to serve you at all times, and do you not want to give one hour or two hours to devotion to the Lord? Let your sloth therefore be chastised, so that the earth may not lose its produce. The sword will be brought upon the works of the hands of those by whom God is not heard in the churches.

Our sloth condemns us, my brothers. The Jew runs in the morning to the synagogue, the pagan hurries and keeps watch at the temple, and the Christian does not keep watch or hurry to the church. It is a great shame for Christians that they are provoked to come to the house of God by a worse example and spectacle, so that the Jew is more sacrilegious in his observance than the Christian is devout in his religion. The profane gentile keeps watch at his idols, and the Christian, for whom Christ was crucified, does not keep watch or hurry to the church. For this reason God chastises the earth, so that man may receive discipline: so that man may be corrected, the land [...] to say. You make my house deserted, and I will make your land deserted. You do not give me honour by coming to me, and I will cut off your labour: because whoever honours me, he says, I too will honour him.

But perhaps you will say to me: I am rich, and abound in all resources, I lack nothing; what can I ask for? Are you rich, then, of yourself? Or were you born with riches? Rather, the richer you are, the more you ought to rise early [and go] to him whose riches they are: because the gold and the silver are mine, he says, and I will give it to whom I wish. Do you have what you did not receive? If then you received it, why do you boast as if you had not received it? Certainly, if you received it, you had nothing, because you came naked from your mother's womb into this world, covered in rags, worn out by extreme want, and, as one born, already bound to die. You have as witness blessed Job, saying: Naked I came out of my mother's belly, naked I must go into the earth. You run to the moneylender's house, you compose flattering words, and do you not run to the house of God, the free giver? What is this great sloth in you, my brothers, that you do not keep watch at all for the house of God? I say to you, whoever you are, lazy countryman: you are too lazy to come to the house of God, and are you not too lazy to work your land? And unless he gives you rain from above, you will not be able to break the ground. It will be able to supply nothing to you of its own, unless it receives from above. For it is written: It comes down from above, from the Father of lights, with whom there is no change nor shadow of alteration. As it is also written in the Gospel: But seek first the kingdom of God and justice, and all these things will be added to you. Therefore, my brothers, you ought to keep watch for the church of God. This is what God awaits: only that you confess to him, and there is no delay to your being healed, for he will ask only for your confession. The end.
